comments.text: My husband and his brothers were all born on Fidalgo Island, we relocated here in 1984, because we wanted to live close to my in laws, because we were starting our family. We like to take the International Ferry to Sydney on Vancouver Island, then tour Victoria or go to Buchart Gardens. Our 3 sons were all born and raised in Anacortes, it was heaven, our kids met their friends in Preschool through High School. Now our 3 grandchildren have started school at the same Elementary School our oldest son, started at, Island View, in the Challenge Program for gifted (very intelligent) that our oldest son spent 5 years in. I don’t like to advertise the San Juan Islands, it was a rule in the 80’s & 90’s we were not supposed to tell people in California about Anacortes, but the cat got out of the bag long ago. Now it’s to well known. And yes, it’s late November, there are horrible storms all up the West Coast, but we are protected by the Olympic Peninsula, and it’s sunny and warm, not a cloud in the sky. comments.text: I would like to come in and say that, yes the problem is real, but this is 2026 and we know these issues can be mitigated. Tourism is not something we need to be scared of, and for most places these issues are easy to deal with. Even for more extreme cases like San Juan county (and I hesitate to call them extreme considering how many people can afford to live there), rich problems beget rich solutions. Need a community ready to serve? Have better zoning laws and rent caps within certain areas. Alaska has a city that literally lives in one building, no excuse to not grow upward rather than outward. The freshwater issue is less straightforward to solve but is almost certainly cheaper to solve than other issues, especially considering how freshwater-rich the surrounding region is. Altogether, it could probably triple in population and be more than fine with some common sense policy. Worst case scenario, rich people are forced back to the communities that gave them their wealth and the nature on the islands is allowed to recover, I see no downside here.

comments.author: @jimjenner
comments.text: Correction, the rain shadow is not from the Canadian mountains on Vancouver Island.  The Olympic Mountains in Washington State to the SouthWest protect the San Juans from rain clouds moving in the prevailing counterclock-wise weather patterns moving down from Alaska.  Small point, but the rain shadow created by the Olympics starts at Sequim in Washington and continues to the Northeast up into the San Juans.
